h1: What a beer label must show: the rules most markets share
title: What a Beer Label Must Show | Craft Beer School
desc: The items most markets require on a beer label: name, strength, volume, producer, origin, allergens, batch code and warnings. Check your own market's rules.
teaser: Label rules differ by country, but the same few items turn up almost everywhere. Know them before you design.
standfirst: A label is a legal document before it is a design. This guide lists what most markets ask for. Your own regulator has the final word.
sections:
A label that breaks the rules can stop a shipment, force a recall or delay a launch. Fixing it after printing is costly. Design with the rules in front of you. Rules differ by country and region and change, so check with the national regulator or a licensing adviser.

Start by asking three questions of every market. Which authority sets the rules? Does it approve labels before sale? What language must the text be in? The answers shape your design, your timeline and your printing choice.

Most markets expect the product name or brand, a description such as beer, lager or ale, the alcohol content by volume, the net volume in the local unit and the name and address of the producer or importer. Many also ask for the country of origin.

Some markets ask for a batch or lot code and a best-before or production date. Check the format they accept.

Volume units differ. Some markets use millilitres, others fluid ounces. The statement may need to follow a set format and minimum character height. Alcohol strength may be shown as a percentage of alcohol by volume, with limits on how precise or rounded it can be.

The producer or importer address must usually be real and contactable. A post office box may not be accepted.

Many markets require allergens to be shown, for example cereals containing gluten. Some ask for a full ingredient list or nutrition information. Rules for alcoholic drinks sometimes differ from those for food. Do not assume your home rules apply abroad.

Allergen rules can catch brewers out. Barley, wheat and rye are cereals containing gluten. Some markets require them to be named, even though beer is a fermented product. Adjuncts such as lactose, nuts or fruit may need declaring too. List every ingredient you use before you design the label.

Nutrition panels and energy values are required for alcoholic drinks in some markets and exempt in others. If you choose to show calories, make sure the figure is tested or calculated properly and that you follow the local format. A wrong number is a compliance problem.

Some countries require health warnings, for example about drinking in pregnancy or while driving, with set rules on wording, size and placement. Others require a responsible drinking message or a recycling mark. Some restrict images that appeal to young people. Never imply that drinking improves health or performance.

Responsible drinking statements are common. Plain wording is usually better than clever wording. Do not suggest that drinking solves problems or improves success. Do not design a label that looks aimed at children.

Several markets review labels before sale. In the United States, the TTB reviews many beer labels. Elsewhere, an importer or a national body may do it. Allow time in your plan. See brewery licensing: the steps most countries share.

Alcohol content may need to be shown within a permitted tolerance. Test your beer, not just the recipe target.

Keep a file for each label version: the artwork, the approval, the date and the batch numbers it was used on. If a regulator asks, you can show exactly what was on shelf.

Imports add steps. The importer may need to hold a licence and may have to register the label or the product. Ask your importer what they need from you. Send artwork files early so there is time to correct them.

Sales channels matter too. Beer sold in shops, bars and online may face different requirements. Kegs often have separate rules for the label or tag on the keg.
Design with the rules in mind

Leave space for mandatory text at a readable size, in the right language or languages. Keep a separate back label for the details if the front needs to stay clean. Cans, bottles and kegs have different surfaces and different needs.

See protecting a beer name in more than one country, can or bottle for hot markets and marketing non-alcoholic beer in the Gulf for neighbouring decisions.

Check the proof from your printer against the rules before the full run. Small errors, such as a missing unit or a clipped warning, can force a reprint of thousands.
faqs: Do all countries require the same label items?
No. Many items are common, but the wording, size, language and extra warnings differ. Check each market.
It varies. Some markets require approval by the regulator before sale. Others rely on the importer. Ask your regulator or adviser.
Can I print one label for several countries?
Sometimes, if the differences are small and you leave space for stickers or local text. Many brands print market-specific versions.
